title: Increased spread of global flash droughts threatens vegetation productivity resilience

paper_content.abstract: Flash drought (faster-developing drought) has been pervasively intensified, posing detrimental constraints on vegetation productivity. However, the potential expansion of flash droughts from flash drought hotspots to non-hotspots and its associated risks to vegetation productivity remain unknown. Furthermore, the divergence in the underlying drivers governing vegetation productivity responses to flash and slow droughts (slower-developing droughts) is unclear. We quantify the dominant drivers underlying vegetation productivity resilience (the departure of productivity anomalies after drought effect to the long-term mean) to both flash and slow droughts. There exhibits significantly lower productivity resilience to flash drought at flash drought hotspots than non-hotspots (Δ = -0.07 ± 0.02, t = -3.25, p < 0.001). The productivity resilience to flash drought is more sensitive to the same reduction in productivity anomaly and intensified climate stress than slow drought. Carbon dioxide fertilization effect exerts the greatest positive effect on productivity resilience to both flash and slow droughts, although that effect is smaller under flash droughts. Our study underscores the limited global ecosystem resilience to the intensification and spread of flash droughts.
paper_content.introduction:
Flash droughts are becoming increasingly pervasive accompanied with climate warming and intensification of human activities 1-5. In recent years, rapid intensification of flash droughts has been reported across the United States 6, Europe 7, Sahel 2, China 8 and Australia 9, that significantly impacted agricultural productivity and terrestrial carbon sink 10, 11. The intensification of flash droughts is mainly attributed to complicated interactions of warmer temperature-induced increased water demands 12 and deficit in precipitation supply 1, 13, which increases evapotranspiration 4, 14. Compared with slow droughts, flash droughts are characterized with exceptionally high onset speed and acute depletion of soil water availability within an extremely short time at sub-seasonal timescales 1, 6, 11, 15, 16. Flash droughts have more detrimental effects on vegetation and carbon sequestration than slow droughts 10, 11, 13. However, a comprehensive understanding of the potential divergence in and the underlying drivers for the drought resilience of vegetation productivity to flash and slow droughts at broad scale remains lacking, which are essential for better prediction of the critical consequences of flash drought intensification.

Flash droughts impose pervasively detrimental effects on vegetation productivity across different biomes 10, 11, 13. In response to flash drought, vegetation quickly loses water into the air, thus exacerbating the rapid decline in soil moisture and plant hydraulic function 11, 13. In contrast, slow drought is characterized by a slower soil moisture decline, with relatively mild climate stress 1. A persistent warming and drying trend tends to tightly associate with loss in vegetation resilience 17. Increasing evidences report that vegetation resilience is susceptible to extreme climate events (e.g., extreme drought, heatwaves) and seasonality of water availability 18, 19. Nonetheless, the potential divergence in the resilience of vegetation productivity to flash and slow drought remains unknown, such as higher or lower resilience under flash droughts 20. Additionally, a comprehensive understanding of the potential expansion of flash drought spatiotemporally remains unconclusive, while previous studies mostly focus on the flash drought hotspots 1, 2, where flash droughts prevail. We know even less about the potential expansions of flash droughts from flash drought hotspots to non-hotspots (see Methods), and what impacts on vegetation resilience emerge. We particularly concentrate on the consequences of intensified flash droughts on vegetation productivity resilience, which is central and essential for comprehensive assessment of the detrimental impacts of widespread flash droughts on ecosystem functioning and hence the human well-being.

Here, we map the count, severity, and onset speed of both flash and slow droughts globally from 1950 to 2023. Flash drought hotspots are then identified by integrating all three metrics (see Methods). We investigate the global pattern and underlying drivers of the responses of vegetation productivity to both flash and slow droughts, leveraging on gridded GPP (gross primary productivity) and SIF (sun-induced fluorescence) data and Fluxnet site observations. We further capture the divergence in vegetation productivity responses to flash and slow droughts during the growing seasons by calculating resilience (i.e., the mean of vegetation anomaly after the drought effect) in the period of 2001 – 2019. Different random forest models are applied to evaluate the importance of diverse factors to vegetation productivity resilience. Specifically, the main objectives are to: (1) characterize the spatiotemporal intensification of global flash drought; (2) determine the divergence in vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts, and (3) identify the drivers underlying vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts.
paper_content.results:
Spatiotemporal patterns in flash drought
We first quantified the spatiotemporal patterns in the occurrence of flash and slow droughts from 1950 to 2023. The flash and slow droughts were determined by the decline in onset speed, with flash drought having no less than 5% in percentile for each pentad and slow drought having at least one pentad with the decline rate of less than 5% in percentile (see Methods). The counts, onset speed and severity of flash drought exhibited great spatial heterogeneity. There exhibited a larger number of more severe flash drought events in the western and southern parts of the Amazon, the western Sahel and tropical Southeast Asia (Figure 1a – c). Regions with higher mean annual precipitation and evaporation exhibited greater flash drought counts, higher severity and faster onset speed (Figure 1d – f). Temporally, we observed significant increasing trends in the anomalies of flash drought counts (6.63 ± 0.66 counts yr-1, z = 5.01, p < 0.001), severity (0.01 ± 0.01% yr-1, z = 4.80, p < 0.001) and onset speed (0.02 ± 0.01% / pentad yr-1, z = 5.66, p < 0.001) during 1950 – 2023, with a rapid acceleration occurring after the turning point in the early 21st century (Figure 1g – i). Although the means severity and onset speed of slow drought also increased rapidly (0.01 ± 0.01% yr-1, z = 4.96 and 0.01 ± 0.01% / pentad yr-1, z = 6.84; both p < 0.001) (Figure S1), which were both weaker than flash drought. The ratio of flash droughts to total drought events is accelerating during 1950 – 2023 (0.14 ± 0.09%, z = 6.16, p < 0.001) (Figure S2).

There were notable differences in the anomalies of multiple climate factors at the onset stage between flash and slow droughts. Compared with slow drought, flash drought exhibited significantly greater mean negative anomaly in precipitation (Δ = -0.296 ± 0.004 mm d-1, t = -73.58, p < 0.001). The mean positive anomalies in temperature (Δ = 0.52 ± 0.01 °C d-1, t = 50.97, p < 0.001), radiation (Δ = 5.59 ± 0.07 J m-2 d-1, t = 82.11, p < 0.001), vapor pressure deficit (Δ = 0.63 ± 0.01 hPa d-1, t = 44.55, p < 0.001) and evaporation (Δ = 0.095 ± 0.001 mm d-1, t = 66.84, p < 0.001) were significantly greater during flash drought than during slow drought. Interestingly, flash droughts were associated with a mean higher soil moisture anomaly than slow droughts (Δ = 0.0014 ± 0.0001 m3 m-3 d-1, t = 30.56, p < 0.001) (Figure S3a – f). Consistent patterns in the anomalies of climate factors between flash and slow droughts were also confirmed by Fluxnet observations (Figure S3g – l).

We then identified global hotspots of flash drought based on the magnitude of MFDI (see Methods), which integrates three metrics of the flash drought. A higher magnitude of MFDI over 100 indicates that flash drought events are relatively more frequent, severe, and fast-developed during the onset phase (Figure S4a, b), and thus regions with MFDI higher than 100 can be considered as the flash drought hotspots (Figure S4c). The identified flash drought hotspots mainly encompassed humid regions (i.e., aridity index ≥ 0.65) (99.46%), whereas the non-hotspots comprised 33.58% humid regions and 66.42% non-humid regions (Figure 2a). Flash drought hotspots had significantly higher MFDI (102.29 ± 10.13) than non-hotspots (92.94 ± 15.57) (t = 38.36, p < 0.001) (Figure 2b). Interestingly, there were significantly lower trends in MFDI at flash drought hotspots than non-hotspots (Δ Kendall’s τ = -0.01 ± 0.001, t = -7.07, p < 0.001) from 1950 to 2023 (Figure 2c).

Divergence in vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts
We quantified and compared the GPP resilience to flash and slow droughts. The GPP resilience is quantified by the difference between mean GPP anomalies within two years after the drought and the multi-year mean growing season GPP. Global GPP showed lower resilience to flash drought than slow drought (Δ = -0.012 ± 0.004, t = -2.74, p < 0.01), and regions with lower GPP resilience to flash drought than that to slow drought are mainly located in North America, central Asia, eastern Europe and central Australia (Figure 3a). The mean GPP resilience to flash drought was significantly higher than that to slow drought (Δ = 0.04 ± 0.02, t = 2.45, p < 0.01) at flash drought hotspots (Figure 3b). However, an opposite pattern was observed in GPP resilience (Δ = -0.05 ± 0.02, t = -2.38, p < 0.01) at non-hotspots (Figure 3b). We further found that the GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts at flash drought hotspots was significantly lower than that at non-hotspots (Δ = -0.07 ± 0.02, t = -3.25 and Δ = -0.15 ± 0.02, t = -8.80; both p < 0.001) (Figure 3b). Consistent patterns were observed from the SIF data (Figure S5) and verified by Fluxnet site observations (Figure S6).

Drivers of vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts
The random forest models were applied to investigate the association of vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts with hydro-meteorological conditions, CO2 fertilization effect (β, defined as ∂Productivity/∂CO2), vegetation response features, plant functional trait, stand features and soil property. In this study, 15 factors were introduced to attribute the vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts at the pentad scale (see Methods). Partial dependence analysis was performed to quantify the impacts of different factors on vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts, respectively.

We explored and compared the underlying drivers of GPP resilience to flash and slow droughts. The CO2 fertilization effect was the most important individual factor for GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts (Figure 4a; Figure 5a). GPP resilience to flash droughts was less sensitive to increasing CO2 fertilization effect than slow drought (Figure 4b; Figure 5b). GPP resilience to flash drought was more sensitive to decrease in the GPP anomalies during and preceding droughts than slow drought at flash drought hotspots, with this pattern fading at non-hotspots (Figure 4c, f; Figure 5c, g). Along with increase in radiation, temperature and evaporation and decrease in the water availability, the GPP resilience to flash drought exhibited a more rapid decline than that to slow drought at flash drought hotspots (Figure 4e, g – k). Climate factors in together have the highest contribution to GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts at non-hotspots (39.07 ± 3.86% and 34.72 ± 2.64%, respectively). GPP resilience showed more sensitive to intensified climate stress brought by flash drought than slow drought (Figure 5e, f, h, k). The shallower maximum rooting depth was associated with much lower GPP resilience to slow drought than to flash drought at flash drought hotspots (Figure 4d), while GPP resilience showed less sensitive to the increase in maximum rooting depth during flash drought than during slow drought at non-hotspots (Figure 5d). Soil property exerts marginal effects on GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts. Consistent patterns were observed in the SIF dataset (Figure S7; Figure S8).
paper_content.methods:
Ecosystem variables
In this study, vegetation productivity was investigated via a daily gross primary productivity (GPP) dataset, which was directly obtained from FluxSat (2001 – 2019) (https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/catalog/ornl-cloud-fluxsat-gpp-fpar-1835-2) 43. We also used 4-day solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) data from the CSIF dataset (2001 – 2019) (https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/CSIF/6387494) for supplementary analyses 44. FluxSat data was derived from the MODIS using the nadir bidirectional reflectance distribution function production (MCD43C4) as input to neural networks that were used to upscale the GPP estimated at flux sites 43. FluxSat dataset has considered the differences in CO2 absorption efficiency between C3 and C4 vegetation 43. Specifically, vegetation was separated into two classes using satellite measurements: (1) highly productive (e.g., in crop regions such as C4 maize with high relative annual maximum GPP values) and (2) all others (e.g., C3 vegetation) 43. FluxSat dataset has been widely used for vegetation response to drought in previous studies 49, 50. The native spatial resolution of the FluxSat GPP data is 0.05 degree. The CSIF dataset is produced based on SIF retrievals from OCO-2 and surface reflectance data derived from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) onboard the Terra and Aqua satellites (0.05 degrees) 44. We used the simple average method to scale the raw data (GPP and SIF) up to 1 degree for matching the gridded climate data. We also linearly interpolated the SIF data (4-days) to the daily scale and then aggregated the daily GPP and SIF data to 5-day (pentad) mean data after deseasonalization and detrending. We also applied Fluxnet site level flux observation dataset (FLUXNET2015, https://fluxnet.org/data/fluxnet2015-dataset/) 45 to further validate our findings. We discarded sites without recorded flash drought and slow drought events. The vegetation type was determined from the international geosphere biosphere program classification in MCD12C1 (https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data) 51. In the upscaling process, we used the mode value in the upscaling window to express the vegetation type.

Stand features and plant trait, including the tree density, canopy height and maximum rooting depth, are physiologically associated with plant water transport and use. The tree density determines the intensity of competition in forests and was derived from a global tree density map (https://elischolar.library.yale.edu/yale_fes_data/1/) 52. The canopy height is closely related to vegetation productivity, and was derived from the global 1-km canopy height map dataset (https://lidar.jpl.nasa.gov/data/general.php) 53. The maximum rooting depth affects vegetation productivity resilience to environmental stress and the dataset was derived from the Global Earth Observation for Integrated Water Resource Assessment platform (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/603608) 47.

Climate and soil property data
Daily gridded climate data from 1950 – 2023 were obtained from the ERA5_Land dataset of Copernicus (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/dataset/reanalysis-era5-land?tab=overview) 54, including the air temperature at 2 m above the global surface, downward shortwave solar radiation, total precipitation, evaporation, soil moisture (0 – 7 cm, 7 – 28 cm, and 28 – 100 cm), and 2-m dewpoint temperature. These daily climate data exhibit a spatial resolution of 0.1 degree, which we scaled up to 1 degree (by using the simple average method). On the basis of the ERA5_Land climate dataset, we calculated the vapor pressure deficit 55. We additionally obtained daily soil moisture (0 – 1 m) data from the GLDAS_CLSM dataset (resampled 0.25 degree to 1 degree) 56. The snow water equivalent derived from the GLDAS_CLSM dataset was introduced in our study (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets?keywords=GLDAS) 56. We compiled simulated daily soil moisture (0 – 1 m) data from nine earth system models, which are available in CMIP6 project (https://aims2.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/) 57, to analyze future flash drought pattern. Firstly, we chose the SSP245 scenario which is the most likely scenario to occur in the future 28. Secondly, all the models are with appropriate spatio-temporal resolution for the future analysis. Thirdly, we applied the nearest neighbor method to resample the original simulations into 1 degree and took the 5-day soil moisture mean to capture future flash and slow droughts. Fourthly, we evaluated the performance in soil moisture simulation of flash drought counts across the nine models by Taylor plot (Figure S15). On the premise of ensuring high correlation, we removed the model with lower levels of standard deviation and root mean square deviation (CMCC_CM2_SR5). Finally, we used simulation data of eight earth system models (mrso; r1i1p1f1; model names: ACCESS-CM2, BCC-CSM2-MR, MIROC6, MPPI-ESM1-2-HR, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, MRI-ESM2-0, NorESM2-LM and NorESM2-MM) of the CMIP6 under the SSP245 scenario (Table S3). Daily atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration observation dataset was obtained from Global Monitoring Laboratory platform (https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/).

The soil cation exchange capacity indicate the soil capacity for nutrient retention. It was obtained directly from the Regridded Harmonized World Soil Database v.1.2 (https://gaez.fao.org/pages/hwsd) 58.

Identification of flash and slow droughts
We defined flash and slow droughts on the basis of soil moisture changes 1. To capture grid-level flash and slow droughts accurately, we used two distinct soil moisture datasets (ERA5_Land and GLDAS_CLSM). The depth-weighted average was calculated for the ERA5_Land soil moisture data (0 – 7 cm, 7 – 28 cm, and 28 – 100 cm) to get 1-m soil moisture 1. The depth-weighted average soil moisture was calculated using Equation 1:
SM = (0.07×SM1 + 0.21×SM2 + 0.72×SM3) (1)
SM indicated the weighted mean soil moisture. SM1, SM2 and SM3 indicated soil moisture of 0 – 7 cm, 7 – 28 cm and 28 – 100 cm, respectively. GLDAS_CLSM soil moisture data based on the global land surface model for the top 1 m depth were also used. We then calculated the mean values of the two datasets to reduce the potential bias. The mean soil moisture data were applied in the following analyses. In each grid pixel, the soil moisture was aggregated into a 5-day average (pentad), which was then converted into percentiles. We further identified flash and slow droughts during the growing seasons in the period of 1950 – 2023 (Figure S16). The flash drought was identified by four rules: (1) the pentad-mean soil moisture decreases from above the 40th percentile to the 20th percentile, with the decline rate of no less than 5% in percentile for each pentad; (2) once the soil moisture drops below the 20th percentile, the flash drought onset ends if the decline rate of a pentad is less than 5% in percentile; (3) if the soil moisture rises above the 20th percentile again, the flash drought terminates; and (4) flash drought lasted at least 4 pentads. Slow drought events were identified as follows: (1) the pentad-mean soil moisture decreases from above the 40th percentile to the 20th percentile, with at least one pentad having the decline rate of less than 5% in percentile; (2) when the soil moisture drops below the 20th percentile, the slow drought onset ends if the soil moisture starts to increase; (3) if the soil moisture rises above the 20th percentile again, the slow drought terminates; and (4) slow drought lasted at least 4 pentads.

Flash and slow droughts differ in the onset speed, of which flash drought exhibits the decline rate of no less than 5% in percentile for each pentad at the onset stage 1. The onset speed was defined as the mean decline rate of the pentad-mean soil moisture percentile at the onset stage, which was the difference between the 40th percentile and the lowest percentile at the onset stage divided by the length of onset 1. The severity was defined as the difference between the 40th percentile and the lowest percentile at the onset stage 25. The flash drought ratio was calculated as the ratio of the flash drought counts to the sum of flash and slow droughts from 1950 to 2023 1. We used the Bayesian change point detection (BEAST) model to automatically detect abrupt turning points of the interannual variation in flash and slow droughts 59.

We also introduced the land-atmosphere coupling index (CSI_SM-VPD) 60, 61. This index can be expressed as follows:
CSI_SM-VPD = corr(SM, VPD) × σ(VPD) (2)
where corr(SM, VPD) is the Pearson correlation coefficient between the pentad-scale soil moisture and vapor pressure deficit during the drought, σ(VPD) is the standard deviation of vapor pressure deficit, and a smaller CSI means a stronger land-atmosphere coupling state.

Division of flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots
We optimized the method to identify flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots on the basis of previous studies 2, 5. We first defined energy-limited and water-limited regions based on the basis of the ecosystem limitation index (Figure S17a). Ecosystem limitation index was calculated by subtracting the correlation between soil moisture and evapotranspiration from the correlation between the temperature and evapotranspiration 62. An ecosystem limitation index value greater than 0 indicates a water-limited region, and an index value less than 0 indicates an energy-limited region. We then used the aridity index to divide the study regions into four large climate regions 48, including arid (aridity index < 0.2), semi-arid (0.2 ≤ aridity index < 0.5), sub-humid (0.5 ≤ aridity index < 0.65) and humid (aridity index ≥ 0.65) regions (Figure S17b). Next, we divided our study region into forest, shrub, crop and grass regions based on the vegetation type map (Figure S17c). Finally, we took the spatial intersection among the patterns of the above three global divisions into 29 regions (e.g., humid forest in energy limited region). Each region is defined by unique vegetation type, moisture and energy conditions, which means these regions exhibit different risks when facing drought stress.

We applied multivariate flash drought indicator (MFDI) to determine the flash drought hotspots 25. The MFDI can be calculated as follows:
Let X = x_ij be the matrix with n rows (representing the number of global grids) and m columns (representing flash drought ratio, counts, severity, and onset speed) and, the standardized matrix, Z = z_ij is then given as:
z_ij = 100 ± ((x_ij - M_xj) / S_xj) × 10 (3)
where Z is transformed using a common scale with mean = 100 and standardized deviation = 10, M_xj and S_xj denote the mean and the standard deviation of the jth indicator given as:
M_xj = (∑_{i=1}^n x_ij) / n (4)
S_xj = √(∑_{i=1}^n (x_ij - M_xj)^2 / n) (5)
Let cv_i be the coefficient of variation for the ith unit:
cv_i = S_zi / M_zi (6)
where M_zi = (∑_{j=1}^m z_ij) / m, S_zi = √(∑_{j=1}^m (z_ij - M_zi)^2 / m)
Then, the generalized form of MFDI is given by:
MFDI = M_zi ± S_zi * cv_i (7)
For each region, we calculated the average value of MFDI and compared it to 100. The regions with the average value of MFDI higher than 100 were defined as flash drought hotspots. Conversely, we defined as non-hotspots.

Responses of vegetation productivity to drought
We quantified the vegetation productivity responses to flash and slow droughts following a conceptual diagram (Figure S18). There are two patterns of post-drought recovery: one growing season recovery and multiple growing season recovery 48. Previous studies have shown that vegetation normally recovers within 2 years after drought disturbance 63, 64. Therefore, we discarded drought events with intervals between two droughts shorter than 2 years. We captured almost exclusively drought events where the vegetation time series showed positive anomaly before the drought’s occurrence and showed negative anomaly during the drought. We only considered the flash drought occurred during growing season and both post-drought recovery patterns of vegetation productivity. The pixel-specific growing season was determined by a pixel-specific threshold of the minimum value plus 30% of the seasonal amplitude fitting for the multiyear averaged GPP 48, 65-68. The growing season identification was further verified with SIF (Figure S19). We investigated vegetation changes within two years after drought cessation to explore the response processes of vegetation productivity to flash and slow droughts. We considered the recovery of vegetation productivity from the maximum negative anomaly point to the multi-year growing season mean state within 2 years to be the recovery process under drought effect. The resilience was quantified as the mean of vegetation anomalies after the drought effect (Y_a) minus the multi-year growing season mean (Y_m) (Equation 8) 69. A resilience value lower than 0 indicates that the effect of the drought event persists after disturbance, with lower values indicating weaker resilience.
Resilience = Y_a - Y_m (8)

Attribution analysis
We established four random forest attribution models for flash and slow droughts at flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots, respectively. In each attribution model, the importances of different factors were evaluated. We considered 15 factors in the attribution analyses, which can be grouped into 6 categories, including climate factors (spatio-temporal), CO2 fertilization effect (spatio-temporal), vegetation response features (spatio-temporal), soil property (spatial), plant trait (spatial) and stand features (spatial). All factors with temporal dimension were deseasonalized and detrended. Multiple climate factors during the drought response period (i.e., the period from the beginning of drought to the maximum vegetation negative anomaly) were considered, including the mean values of temperature, radiation, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, soil moisture and evaporation (Figure S20). Non-growing season snow anomalies could affect the spring phenology and further alter the post-drought vegetation recovery pattern across growing seasons 70. Thus, we included the non-growing season snow water equivalent. We also considered the mean values of vegetation productivity during the drought response period. Previous studies revealed that the vegetation state during the two months preceding a flash drought could compensate for the vegetation recovery process 39, 71, 72. Therefore, we also introduced the mean GPP of this period into our final random forest models. Soil property (soil cation exchange capacity), plant trait (maximum rooting depth) and stand features (canopy height and tree density) were also included in the final model. Besides, we considered the CO2 fertilization effect (β) 30, which is defined as the relative increase in vegetation productivity in response to the increase in atmospheric CO2 concentration and determined as follows:
β = ∂Productivity/∂CO2 (9)
Many studies have pointed out that the increase of CO2 can promote the plant water use efficiency 29, 73. Therefore, we included water use efficiency into the attribution analyses to assess the indirect impacts of CO2 fertilization effects on vegetation productivity resilience based on Equation 10.
WUE = Productivity / Evapotranspiration (10)
Prior to performing the final attribution models, VIF was used to test the collinearity among factors, and the factors with a larger VIF (VIF > 5) were removed to prevent the confusion effects (Figure S21a) 74.

The random forest model provides the advantages of high prediction accuracy, high robustness, accurate factor interpretation and ease of use 46. Separate random forest models were constructed to investigate the differences in the drivers underlying vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts at flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots. Here, we defined that each random forest had 300 binary trees with 5 leaves. The R2 value of the random forest attribution models were all above 0.80 (Figure S21b – e). A factor importance ranking was obtained via the permutation importance method based on Out-of-Bag data, with values normalized. The permutation feature importance method is a model inspection technique applicable for any fitted model and is especially useful for nonlinear models. The importance of permutation features is defined as the decrease in model accuracy when a single feature value is randomly perturbed. The larger the decrease after the permutation, the greater the importance of this factor 75. We selected the top ten factors as major factors for further analyses. Partial dependence plot was used to characterize the relationship between each factor and vegetation productivity resilience 76.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript NCOMMS-25_04110 aims to understand the mechanism explaining the divergent responses of GPP to flash vs. slow droughts by quantifying the contributions of various environmental factors to the GPP change under droughts. Global-scale estimations of flash/slow droughts and the GPP resilience between 1950-2023 have been mapped based on 1m-deep reanalysis soil moisture time series. The manuscript is well-organized overall and has a clear structure. The results agree with the previously reported increasing spread of flash droughts and present insights into the understanding and prediction of the ecosystem's response to the changing climate. However, the result section should be written in a way that is more cohesive and concise. Its current form may emphasize reporting the outcomes of data analysis more than backing up the arguments. I also have some questions regarding the methodology and authors' interpretation of their results. Please see my detailed comments below.
1. Abstract lines 25-27 If increased CO2 strongly drives the vegetation growth resilience to both flash and slow droughts, you should delete the other half of the sentence "...a smaller effect on vegetation growth resilience to flash drought" or revise it as something like "...although that effect is smaller with regard to flash drought compared to slow drought "
2. Abstract lines 27-30: What does "deterioration in vegetation and hydrothermal factor" mean?
3. Abstract lines 27-30: Are flash drought non-hotspots the same as slow drought hotspots? What is the response of vegetation growth resilience to slow drought hotspots (decreased or no effect?) and why did CO2 still explain most of this response?
3. Regarding Figure 5a and key point #2 lines 39-41 "...whereas the effect on vegetation growth resilience to flash drought was smaller". Are relative contributions of drivers comparable between RF models? Did you specify the leaf node of each tree, the bootstrapping and the shuffle procedures to make the structure of RF models identical? The relative importance values can be compared within a model, but not across models, to give the relative rank of various drivers. A larger relative importance of a specific driver in the slow drought model than that in the flash drought model may not necessarily indicate the effect of that driver on the GPP resilience to slow drought is smaller than in the case of slow drought.
4. Key point#3: Why "climate factors provided the highest explanatory power at non-hotspots"? Maybe briefly touch on the mechanisms?
5. Figure 1: Please make sure the units and legend color are consistent for each variable across panels. a and d have different color schemes (yellow-red vs. blue-red) for the drought counts. b and e have different units (90 vs. 0.9) for the drought ratio. c and f have different legend text ("%/pentad" vs "Onset speed (%/pentad)") for the onset speed.
6. Lines 124-126: Why is soil moisture considered as one of the climate factors in Figure S3?
7. Line 141: Maybe the title could be "Divergence in... responses to flash and slow droughts" since both resilience and resistance were covered in this subsection.
8. lines 401-403: Since you are using GPP to represent the vegetation growth, maybe it's more appropriate to use "vegetation productivity" instead of "vegetation growth" in the title and related main text because ecologists have traditionally used other proxies to represent vegetation growth and vegetation resilience.
9. Methods lines 471-473: Why does the onset stage end at the first 5-day (3rd pentad) when the soil moisture is below the 20th percentile for the flash drought, but at the second 5-day (6th pentad) for the slow drought in Fig S12?
10. Still lines 471-473: But in Fig S12 (a), it's at the end, not the beginning, of the recovery stage (6th pentad) when the soil moisture begins to increase. Suggest deleting "if the soil moisture level began to increase"
11. Lines 478-480: This second rule seems to apply to the slow drought as well.
12. Still lines 478-480: Suggest replacing "onset" with "decline".
13. lines 483-485: Should it be "the 40th percentile" or "the percentile of the last pentad before the onset stage"?
14. Lines 516-517: Did you find drought events during which GPP increased?
15. Lines 517-518: The terms "one growing season recovery" and "multi growing season recovery" were used in Fig S15, please be consistent.
16. Lines 518-520: What about droughts that persist and frequently happen? Any long-term lags, propagation, legacy effect, or memory of soil moisture resulted?
17. Lines 523-524 Please rephrase it and explain which vegetation index was used and what the pixel-specific threshold was used for.
18. Lines 547-549 Did not find the citation for "the previous study".
19. Lines 556-559 What did you compare the correlation coefficient with? Vegetation resilience? What's the purpose of retaining factors with abs(R) less than 0.7? Also, please add the absolute notation in Fig S16.
20. Lines 559: Why vpd was not included? The correlation coefficients between vpd and other factors were also not shown in Fig S16a.

Guo et al quantify drought resistance and resilience of vegetation across the globe. They use a range of vegetation remote sensing datasets like CSIF and FluxSat to characterize these responses of vegetation to flash and slow droughts. They report a range of results including the prevalence of increasing frequency of flash droughts, less resilience of vegetation to flash droughts than slow droughts, and strong relation of CO2 to drought resilience as explained by a random forest model. The methods do appear to be mostly careful and I can appreciate the thought the authors put into those, but in general I had trouble following the large breadth of results. I also question the vegetation response differences claimed between flash and slow drought and hotspots and non hotspots. I think the breadth of results covered here in the analysis are actually a weakness in this case. The analysis could be stronger if more honed on fewer of these arguments so we can gain confidence in the claims. In general, I had trouble following the narrative and am left wondering what the takeaways are. It is unclear if these are addressable issues or not but I do think more work is required here. See my comments below as a guide to improve the manuscript.
Major comments
1. There is very little difference between fast and slow drought response in figure 3. In fact the variability around the medians is very large and I am surprised to see that the differences were found to be statistically significant. Potentially, this is an artifact of having many data points. Which significance test was used here? This issue castes some doubt on the differences for flash and non flash droughts and I am not sure we can confidently make many of these claims in general in lines 142-165 and throughout figure 3. At least they don’t seem like strong arguments.
2. There are many arguments being made throughout the study about flash drought changes in time, differences between slow and fast drought, differences between hotspots and non hotspots, and then the many factors explaining the differences in patterns. I’ll admit I really struggled to follow the story throughout following these different threads. Potentially, one aspect that can help is to merge the results and discussions sections more because so much material is covered in both. It requires a lot of bouncing back and forth between the figures, results text, and discussion text. Another point that can help is to trim out the arguments that aren’t contributing much and focus more on the messages that do.
3. I am suspicious about why there are so many flash droughts in humid locations and so few in dry locations. I in general agree with how the droughts and flash droughts are identified with the different criteria starting in line 469. However, I am unsure about the 5%/pentad definition for flash drought. This should be a relative change and not a magnitude change. Otherwise, dry locations will rarely have high enough soil moisture to lose moisture at this rate. It should be based on a relative change to normalize across different conditions.
4. I am not sure what we are learning from the attribution analysis in Figures 4 and 5. I am admittedly having trouble articulating how I am not following everything but will give a few examples here. First of all, it is unclear whether relationships are being evaluated spatially or temporally and therefore I am not sure how to interpret whether a variable “controls” vegetation drought resilience (as describing spatial gradients, or describing how they respond in time). Second, the perceived processes governing how the variables are related are a bit unclear. The CO2 concentration itself is not considered a fast-acting variable that can directly change a plant response to drought. Effectively, all plants should be experiencing the same mean levels of CO2 because they are well mixed, so I am guessing this analysis is being conducted temporally? Otherwise, water use efficiency or a stomatal trait is potentially more suited in place of CO2. This could be an issue of timescales where CO2 variations have such strong trends compared to the other variables that they are highly related to trends in the drought metrics. As a counterarguement to show my point: if the analysis is conducted over 1-5 years, CO2 may no longer be a large explanatory variable. Finally, the remainder of the variables are so close in their explanatory value that I am not quite clear what we have learned from this analysis. The differences in hotspots and slow and fast drought are so small as well that I don’t think there is much information presented other than we can’t distinguish much from what the attribution analysis is showing.
More specific comments

L92: it would be worth giving context early how flash drought and slow drought differ
L126: again, a definition of what a flash drought hotspot is would be very helpful. It also feels a bit strange to have this seemingly main result all be in the SI
L153: are we just looking at differences of drought response in difference climatic regions?
L157: a definition of resilience and resistance would be helpful
L168-169: in time? In space?
L172: I don’t understand this statement. Is this increasing co2 in time or co2 time variability? It is unclear if these are relationships in time, space, or both
L224-226: the lack of definitions, such as how hotspots are defined, in the main text makes it challenging to follow this discussion
L248-250: maybe the more direct variable acting through co2 is water use efficiency or stomatal strategies (including c3 versus c4)? I am generally struggling to follow how co2 is such a strong factor explaining drought strategies
L392-394: I am not seeing where this result is represented in figure 4
L477: is this 5% by magnitude of soil moisture or a 5% relative change? This makes a big difference and might explain why so few dry locations see flash droughts based on this definition. Soil moisture is already low and near a lower bound and thus is unable to drop 5% by magnitude.
L549-553: are these spatial and temporal changes of these variables? Or just temporal?
Figure 3: the differences reported here are very small. Which significance tests were used?
Figure 4: there aren’t too large of differences between drought and non drought hotspots and I am unclear what to takeaway from this other than conclusions about CO2.

MANUSCRIPT REVIEW for "Increased Spread of Global Flash Drought Threats to Vegetation Growth Resilience"
The paper, by Guo et al., demonstrates good technical proficiency in data analysis, effectively handling multiple datasets to explore flash drought characteristics. However, it falls short in critical areas: the scientific rationale and mechanisms driving the results are largely absent, and the motivation lacks clarity and robustness. Given the significant gaps in scientific justification and contribution, I recommend REJECTION, as these issues undermine the paper’s overall impact and validity.
Major Comments:
The manuscript is difficult to follow, and the flow of the discussion is lacking. The integration of slow and flash droughts is unclear, making it hard to understand the connection between the two. Additionally, the novelty of the work is not well-established, leaving the importance of the study uncertain. Despite citing 90 articles, the manuscript fails to clearly explain the unique contribution of the research. Many of the objectives addressed in the study have already been covered in the cited papers. Furthermore, the discussion of CMIP6 (line 115) seems out of place, as there is no prior explanation of which climate models were selected, how they were chosen, or the methods used for bias correction and downscaling. Additionally, the process of deriving flash droughts (FDs) is not adequately addressed.
The authors have conducted a solid data analysis, demonstrating technical proficiency in their approach. However, a significant limitation undermining the paper’s clarity is the absence of justifications or mechanisms explaining the results. While the methods appear sound, the paper focuses solely on data analysis without exploring the underlying processes driving flash drought characteristics. For instance, the claim that energy-limited regions exhibit the highest FD ratio, decay, and onset rates is presented without subsequent elaboration on why this occurs, particularly in humid regions, and why transitional regions differ. To strengthen the study, I recommend that the authors delve into the scientific rationale—for example, linking findings to physical drivers like evaporative demand, soil-vegetation feedbacks, or regional climate dynamics—in the discussion.
The authors introduce the term "slow drought," but its meaning remains unclear. While droughts are generally understood as slow or creeping phenomena, the paper does not specify whether "slow drought" refers to meteorological, hydrological, or soil moisture drought—or if it encompasses all types. When introducing new terminology, particularly in the abstract or introduction, greater care is needed to provide a precise definition. I recommend that the authors clearly define "slow drought" early in the manuscript to avoid ambiguity and strengthen its scientific grounding.
The motivation and research objectives of the paper are not strong. The introduction starts well by acknowledging previous flash drought work, but it doesn’t discuss mechanisms. Suddenly, the authors bring up the divergence of slow and flash droughts without properly justifying the research gap. The paper would benefit from a more methodical discussion of why this study matters. Based on the introduction, I didn’t find the analysis or research objectives to be clear. A stronger justification for the study’s purpose and contribution would enhance its relevance. I suggest the authors provide a clearer explanation of the significance of their work.
The statement at Line 97, claiming that “energy-limited regions show a significantly high FD ratio,” does not hold for the Eastern USA, a major energy-limited region. Here, the flash drought (FD) ratio ranges from 10% to 15%, which is notably low rather than high. This contradiction undermines the generalization and requires clarification or revision to reflect regional variability accurately. Can the authors explain why this is happening?
A significant drawback of this paper is the heavy reliance on results presented in the supplementary file, with approximately 70% of the discussion referencing supplementary figures. Supplementary material should support, not dominate, the main text by providing additional context for key arguments. Requiring readers to frequently consult the supplementary file disrupts the flow and accessibility of the narrative. I strongly recommend integrating critical supplementary figures into the main manuscript and discussing them there to improve readability and coherence.
The definition of flash drought (FD) hotspots is flawed and requires revision. The authors designate FD hotspots as regions where median values of FD metrics (onset, decay, and FD ratio) exceed the global median, inherently classifying roughly 50% of regions as hotspots (e.g., 46% of global land area in their results). This statistical approach is problematic, as it dilutes the concept of a “hotspot” by encompassing nearly half the globe, rather than pinpointing areas with exceptional FD impact. Hotspots should reflect physically meaningful regions with heightened FD severity—e.g., specific areas like X1, X2, or X3, identified by onset, decay, and intensification rates—rather than a vague percentage of land area. I suggest redefining hotspots based on absolute impact criteria and tying them to distinct geographic regions for clarity and relevance.
The authors utilize multiple predictors, including precipitation, radiation, soil moisture, and available water holding capacity (AWC). I suggest reconsidering the inclusion of AWC, as soil moisture already encapsulates sufficient information about water availability and storage capacity. Incorporating AWC as a separate predictor may introduce redundancy, and its exclusion could streamline the analysis without compromising the results. I recommend justifying its use or removing it to enhance model efficiency.
The font sizes in the figures can be increased for better readability.
In Figure 3, I don’t notice anything significantly different between the hotspot vs. non-hotspot regions. However, the authors state that the results are significantly different across these regions. All the plots in Figure 3 look similar to me. Did the authors perform any statistical significance testing?
Minor Comments:
The title is a little difficult to understand since the phrasing “threats vegetation growth resilience” is used as a verb. I have an alternative suggestion: “Increased Spread of Global Flash Drought Poses a Threat to Vegetation Growth Resilience” or “Increased Spread of Global Flash Droughts Threatens Vegetation Growth Resilience.”
Keywords: "Slow drought" is not a key term. Please change it to “drought.”
Key points (2) and (3) are very large. Please check the allowed maximum length of characters for the key words for Nature Communications. It’s better to split them into two separate key points.
Reference (4) by Satoh et al. is not a flash drought paper but rather a hydrological drought paper. Hence, remove it.
Line 98: When you say “significantly greater,” did you assess this using a statistical significance test, or was it just visually interpreted from the figure?
Figure 1(a, d, g): Instead of writing “times,” simply write “FD counts.” "Times" is not an interpretable word. Be consistent with the figure captions.
Line 449: What do you mean by “cation?”
How did you handle the ERA5 soil moisture data, which are provided at 3 depths? Did you take a weighted average?
(Remarks on code availability)

in scientific justification and contribution, I recommend REJECTION, as these issues
undermine the paper’s overall impact and validity.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Flash drought (faster-developing drought) has been pervasively intensified, posing detrimental constraints on vegetation productivity. However, the potential expansion of flash droughts from flash drought hotspots to non-hotspots and its associated risks to vegetation productivity remain unknown. Furthermore, the divergence in the underlying drivers governing vegetation productivity responses to flash and slow droughts (slower-developing droughts) is unclear. We quantify the dominant drivers underlying vegetation productivity resilience (the departure of productivity anomalies after drought effect to the long-term mean) to both flash and slow droughts. There exhibits significantly lower productivity resilience to flash drought at flash drought hotspots than non-hotspots (Δ = -0.07 ± 0.02, t = -3.25, p < 0.001). The productivity resilience to flash drought is more sensitive to the same reduction in productivity anomaly and intensified climate stress than slow drought. Carbon dioxide fertilization effect exerts the greatest positive effect on productivity resilience to both flash and slow droughts, although that effect is smaller under flash droughts. Our study underscores the limited global ecosystem resilience to the intensification and spread of flash droughts.

---

## Introduction

Flash droughts are becoming increasingly pervasive accompanied with climate warming and intensification of human activities 1-5. In recent years, rapid intensification of flash droughts has been reported across the United States 6, Europe 7, Sahel 2, China 8 and Australia 9, that significantly impacted agricultural productivity and terrestrial carbon sink 10, 11. The intensification of flash droughts is mainly attributed to complicated interactions of warmer temperature-induced increased water demands 12 and deficit in precipitation supply 1, 13, which increases evapotranspiration 4, 14. Compared with slow droughts, flash droughts are characterized with exceptionally high onset speed and acute depletion of soil water availability within an extremely short time at sub-seasonal timescales 1, 6, 11, 15, 16. Flash droughts have more detrimental effects on vegetation and carbon sequestration than slow droughts 10, 11, 13. However, a comprehensive understanding of the potential divergence in and the underlying drivers for the drought resilience of vegetation productivity to flash and slow droughts at broad scale remains lacking, which are essential for better prediction of the critical consequences of flash drought intensification.

Flash droughts impose pervasively detrimental effects on vegetation productivity across different biomes 10, 11, 13. In response to flash drought, vegetation quickly loses water into the air, thus exacerbating the rapid decline in soil moisture and plant hydraulic function 11, 13. In contrast, slow drought is characterized by a slower soil moisture decline, with relatively mild climate stress 1. A persistent warming and drying trend tends to tightly associate with loss in vegetation resilience 17. Increasing evidences report that vegetation resilience is susceptible to extreme climate events (e.g., extreme drought, heatwaves) and seasonality of water availability 18, 19. Nonetheless, the potential divergence in the resilience of vegetation productivity to flash and slow drought remains unknown, such as higher or lower resilience under flash droughts 20. Additionally, a comprehensive understanding of the potential expansion of flash drought spatiotemporally remains unconclusive, while previous studies mostly focus on the flash drought hotspots 1, 2, where flash droughts prevail. We know even less about the potential expansions of flash droughts from flash drought hotspots to non-hotspots (see Methods), and what impacts on vegetation resilience emerge. We particularly concentrate on the consequences of intensified flash droughts on vegetation productivity resilience, which is central and essential for comprehensive assessment of the detrimental impacts of widespread flash droughts on ecosystem functioning and hence the human well-being.

Here, we map the count, severity, and onset speed of both flash and slow droughts globally from 1950 to 2023. Flash drought hotspots are then identified by integrating all three metrics (see Methods). We investigate the global pattern and underlying drivers of the responses of vegetation productivity to both flash and slow droughts, leveraging on gridded GPP (gross primary productivity) and SIF (sun-induced fluorescence) data and Fluxnet site observations. We further capture the divergence in vegetation productivity responses to flash and slow droughts during the growing seasons by calculating resilience (i.e., the mean of vegetation anomaly after the drought effect) in the period of 2001 – 2019. Different random forest models are applied to evaluate the importance of diverse factors to vegetation productivity resilience. Specifically, the main objectives are to: (1) characterize the spatiotemporal intensification of global flash drought; (2) determine the divergence in vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts, and (3) identify the drivers underlying vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts.

---

## Results

Spatiotemporal patterns in flash drought
We first quantified the spatiotemporal patterns in the occurrence of flash and slow droughts from 1950 to 2023. The flash and slow droughts were determined by the decline in onset speed, with flash drought having no less than 5% in percentile for each pentad and slow drought having at least one pentad with the decline rate of less than 5% in percentile (see Methods). The counts, onset speed and severity of flash drought exhibited great spatial heterogeneity. There exhibited a larger number of more severe flash drought events in the western and southern parts of the Amazon, the western Sahel and tropical Southeast Asia (Figure 1a – c). Regions with higher mean annual precipitation and evaporation exhibited greater flash drought counts, higher severity and faster onset speed (Figure 1d – f). Temporally, we observed significant increasing trends in the anomalies of flash drought counts (6.63 ± 0.66 counts yr-1, z = 5.01, p < 0.001), severity (0.01 ± 0.01% yr-1, z = 4.80, p < 0.001) and onset speed (0.02 ± 0.01% / pentad yr-1, z = 5.66, p < 0.001) during 1950 – 2023, with a rapid acceleration occurring after the turning point in the early 21st century (Figure 1g – i). Although the means severity and onset speed of slow drought also increased rapidly (0.01 ± 0.01% yr-1, z = 4.96 and 0.01 ± 0.01% / pentad yr-1, z = 6.84; both p < 0.001) (Figure S1), which were both weaker than flash drought. The ratio of flash droughts to total drought events is accelerating during 1950 – 2023 (0.14 ± 0.09%, z = 6.16, p < 0.001) (Figure S2).

There were notable differences in the anomalies of multiple climate factors at the onset stage between flash and slow droughts. Compared with slow drought, flash drought exhibited significantly greater mean negative anomaly in precipitation (Δ = -0.296 ± 0.004 mm d-1, t = -73.58, p < 0.001). The mean positive anomalies in temperature (Δ = 0.52 ± 0.01 °C d-1, t = 50.97, p < 0.001), radiation (Δ = 5.59 ± 0.07 J m-2 d-1, t = 82.11, p < 0.001), vapor pressure deficit (Δ = 0.63 ± 0.01 hPa d-1, t = 44.55, p < 0.001) and evaporation (Δ = 0.095 ± 0.001 mm d-1, t = 66.84, p < 0.001) were significantly greater during flash drought than during slow drought. Interestingly, flash droughts were associated with a mean higher soil moisture anomaly than slow droughts (Δ = 0.0014 ± 0.0001 m3 m-3 d-1, t = 30.56, p < 0.001) (Figure S3a – f). Consistent patterns in the anomalies of climate factors between flash and slow droughts were also confirmed by Fluxnet observations (Figure S3g – l).

We then identified global hotspots of flash drought based on the magnitude of MFDI (see Methods), which integrates three metrics of the flash drought. A higher magnitude of MFDI over 100 indicates that flash drought events are relatively more frequent, severe, and fast-developed during the onset phase (Figure S4a, b), and thus regions with MFDI higher than 100 can be considered as the flash drought hotspots (Figure S4c). The identified flash drought hotspots mainly encompassed humid regions (i.e., aridity index ≥ 0.65) (99.46%), whereas the non-hotspots comprised 33.58% humid regions and 66.42% non-humid regions (Figure 2a). Flash drought hotspots had significantly higher MFDI (102.29 ± 10.13) than non-hotspots (92.94 ± 15.57) (t = 38.36, p < 0.001) (Figure 2b). Interestingly, there were significantly lower trends in MFDI at flash drought hotspots than non-hotspots (Δ Kendall’s τ = -0.01 ± 0.001, t = -7.07, p < 0.001) from 1950 to 2023 (Figure 2c).

Divergence in vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts
We quantified and compared the GPP resilience to flash and slow droughts. The GPP resilience is quantified by the difference between mean GPP anomalies within two years after the drought and the multi-year mean growing season GPP. Global GPP showed lower resilience to flash drought than slow drought (Δ = -0.012 ± 0.004, t = -2.74, p < 0.01), and regions with lower GPP resilience to flash drought than that to slow drought are mainly located in North America, central Asia, eastern Europe and central Australia (Figure 3a). The mean GPP resilience to flash drought was significantly higher than that to slow drought (Δ = 0.04 ± 0.02, t = 2.45, p < 0.01) at flash drought hotspots (Figure 3b). However, an opposite pattern was observed in GPP resilience (Δ = -0.05 ± 0.02, t = -2.38, p < 0.01) at non-hotspots (Figure 3b). We further found that the GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts at flash drought hotspots was significantly lower than that at non-hotspots (Δ = -0.07 ± 0.02, t = -3.25 and Δ = -0.15 ± 0.02, t = -8.80; both p < 0.001) (Figure 3b). Consistent patterns were observed from the SIF data (Figure S5) and verified by Fluxnet site observations (Figure S6).

Drivers of vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts
The random forest models were applied to investigate the association of vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts with hydro-meteorological conditions, CO2 fertilization effect (β, defined as ∂Productivity/∂CO2), vegetation response features, plant functional trait, stand features and soil property. In this study, 15 factors were introduced to attribute the vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts at the pentad scale (see Methods). Partial dependence analysis was performed to quantify the impacts of different factors on vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts, respectively.

We explored and compared the underlying drivers of GPP resilience to flash and slow droughts. The CO2 fertilization effect was the most important individual factor for GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts (Figure 4a; Figure 5a). GPP resilience to flash droughts was less sensitive to increasing CO2 fertilization effect than slow drought (Figure 4b; Figure 5b). GPP resilience to flash drought was more sensitive to decrease in the GPP anomalies during and preceding droughts than slow drought at flash drought hotspots, with this pattern fading at non-hotspots (Figure 4c, f; Figure 5c, g). Along with increase in radiation, temperature and evaporation and decrease in the water availability, the GPP resilience to flash drought exhibited a more rapid decline than that to slow drought at flash drought hotspots (Figure 4e, g – k). Climate factors in together have the highest contribution to GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts at non-hotspots (39.07 ± 3.86% and 34.72 ± 2.64%, respectively). GPP resilience showed more sensitive to intensified climate stress brought by flash drought than slow drought (Figure 5e, f, h, k). The shallower maximum rooting depth was associated with much lower GPP resilience to slow drought than to flash drought at flash drought hotspots (Figure 4d), while GPP resilience showed less sensitive to the increase in maximum rooting depth during flash drought than during slow drought at non-hotspots (Figure 5d). Soil property exerts marginal effects on GPP resilience to both flash and slow droughts. Consistent patterns were observed in the SIF dataset (Figure S7; Figure S8).

## Methods

Ecosystem variables
In this study, vegetation productivity was investigated via a daily gross primary productivity (GPP) dataset, which was directly obtained from FluxSat (2001 – 2019) (https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/catalog/ornl-cloud-fluxsat-gpp-fpar-1835-2) 43. We also used 4-day solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) data from the CSIF dataset (2001 – 2019) (https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/CSIF/6387494) for supplementary analyses 44. FluxSat data was derived from the MODIS using the nadir bidirectional reflectance distribution function production (MCD43C4) as input to neural networks that were used to upscale the GPP estimated at flux sites 43. FluxSat dataset has considered the differences in CO2 absorption efficiency between C3 and C4 vegetation 43. Specifically, vegetation was separated into two classes using satellite measurements: (1) highly productive (e.g., in crop regions such as C4 maize with high relative annual maximum GPP values) and (2) all others (e.g., C3 vegetation) 43. FluxSat dataset has been widely used for vegetation response to drought in previous studies 49, 50. The native spatial resolution of the FluxSat GPP data is 0.05 degree. The CSIF dataset is produced based on SIF retrievals from OCO-2 and surface reflectance data derived from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) onboard the Terra and Aqua satellites (0.05 degrees) 44. We used the simple average method to scale the raw data (GPP and SIF) up to 1 degree for matching the gridded climate data. We also linearly interpolated the SIF data (4-days) to the daily scale and then aggregated the daily GPP and SIF data to 5-day (pentad) mean data after deseasonalization and detrending. We also applied Fluxnet site level flux observation dataset (FLUXNET2015, https://fluxnet.org/data/fluxnet2015-dataset/) 45 to further validate our findings. We discarded sites without recorded flash drought and slow drought events. The vegetation type was determined from the international geosphere biosphere program classification in MCD12C1 (https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data) 51. In the upscaling process, we used the mode value in the upscaling window to express the vegetation type.

Stand features and plant trait, including the tree density, canopy height and maximum rooting depth, are physiologically associated with plant water transport and use. The tree density determines the intensity of competition in forests and was derived from a global tree density map (https://elischolar.library.yale.edu/yale_fes_data/1/) 52. The canopy height is closely related to vegetation productivity, and was derived from the global 1-km canopy height map dataset (https://lidar.jpl.nasa.gov/data/general.php) 53. The maximum rooting depth affects vegetation productivity resilience to environmental stress and the dataset was derived from the Global Earth Observation for Integrated Water Resource Assessment platform (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/603608) 47.

Climate and soil property data
Daily gridded climate data from 1950 – 2023 were obtained from the ERA5_Land dataset of Copernicus (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/dataset/reanalysis-era5-land?tab=overview) 54, including the air temperature at 2 m above the global surface, downward shortwave solar radiation, total precipitation, evaporation, soil moisture (0 – 7 cm, 7 – 28 cm, and 28 – 100 cm), and 2-m dewpoint temperature. These daily climate data exhibit a spatial resolution of 0.1 degree, which we scaled up to 1 degree (by using the simple average method). On the basis of the ERA5_Land climate dataset, we calculated the vapor pressure deficit 55. We additionally obtained daily soil moisture (0 – 1 m) data from the GLDAS_CLSM dataset (resampled 0.25 degree to 1 degree) 56. The snow water equivalent derived from the GLDAS_CLSM dataset was introduced in our study (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets?keywords=GLDAS) 56. We compiled simulated daily soil moisture (0 – 1 m) data from nine earth system models, which are available in CMIP6 project (https://aims2.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/) 57, to analyze future flash drought pattern. Firstly, we chose the SSP245 scenario which is the most likely scenario to occur in the future 28. Secondly, all the models are with appropriate spatio-temporal resolution for the future analysis. Thirdly, we applied the nearest neighbor method to resample the original simulations into 1 degree and took the 5-day soil moisture mean to capture future flash and slow droughts. Fourthly, we evaluated the performance in soil moisture simulation of flash drought counts across the nine models by Taylor plot (Figure S15). On the premise of ensuring high correlation, we removed the model with lower levels of standard deviation and root mean square deviation (CMCC_CM2_SR5). Finally, we used simulation data of eight earth system models (mrso; r1i1p1f1; model names: ACCESS-CM2, BCC-CSM2-MR, MIROC6, MPPI-ESM1-2-HR, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, MRI-ESM2-0, NorESM2-LM and NorESM2-MM) of the CMIP6 under the SSP245 scenario (Table S3). Daily atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration observation dataset was obtained from Global Monitoring Laboratory platform (https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/).

The soil cation exchange capacity indicate the soil capacity for nutrient retention. It was obtained directly from the Regridded Harmonized World Soil Database v.1.2 (https://gaez.fao.org/pages/hwsd) 58.

Identification of flash and slow droughts
We defined flash and slow droughts on the basis of soil moisture changes 1. To capture grid-level flash and slow droughts accurately, we used two distinct soil moisture datasets (ERA5_Land and GLDAS_CLSM). The depth-weighted average was calculated for the ERA5_Land soil moisture data (0 – 7 cm, 7 – 28 cm, and 28 – 100 cm) to get 1-m soil moisture 1. The depth-weighted average soil moisture was calculated using Equation 1:
SM = (0.07×SM1 + 0.21×SM2 + 0.72×SM3) (1)
SM indicated the weighted mean soil moisture. SM1, SM2 and SM3 indicated soil moisture of 0 – 7 cm, 7 – 28 cm and 28 – 100 cm, respectively. GLDAS_CLSM soil moisture data based on the global land surface model for the top 1 m depth were also used. We then calculated the mean values of the two datasets to reduce the potential bias. The mean soil moisture data were applied in the following analyses. In each grid pixel, the soil moisture was aggregated into a 5-day average (pentad), which was then converted into percentiles. We further identified flash and slow droughts during the growing seasons in the period of 1950 – 2023 (Figure S16). The flash drought was identified by four rules: (1) the pentad-mean soil moisture decreases from above the 40th percentile to the 20th percentile, with the decline rate of no less than 5% in percentile for each pentad; (2) once the soil moisture drops below the 20th percentile, the flash drought onset ends if the decline rate of a pentad is less than 5% in percentile; (3) if the soil moisture rises above the 20th percentile again, the flash drought terminates; and (4) flash drought lasted at least 4 pentads. Slow drought events were identified as follows: (1) the pentad-mean soil moisture decreases from above the 40th percentile to the 20th percentile, with at least one pentad having the decline rate of less than 5% in percentile; (2) when the soil moisture drops below the 20th percentile, the slow drought onset ends if the soil moisture starts to increase; (3) if the soil moisture rises above the 20th percentile again, the slow drought terminates; and (4) slow drought lasted at least 4 pentads.

Flash and slow droughts differ in the onset speed, of which flash drought exhibits the decline rate of no less than 5% in percentile for each pentad at the onset stage 1. The onset speed was defined as the mean decline rate of the pentad-mean soil moisture percentile at the onset stage, which was the difference between the 40th percentile and the lowest percentile at the onset stage divided by the length of onset 1. The severity was defined as the difference between the 40th percentile and the lowest percentile at the onset stage 25. The flash drought ratio was calculated as the ratio of the flash drought counts to the sum of flash and slow droughts from 1950 to 2023 1. We used the Bayesian change point detection (BEAST) model to automatically detect abrupt turning points of the interannual variation in flash and slow droughts 59.

We also introduced the land-atmosphere coupling index (CSI_SM-VPD) 60, 61. This index can be expressed as follows:
CSI_SM-VPD = corr(SM, VPD) × σ(VPD) (2)
where corr(SM, VPD) is the Pearson correlation coefficient between the pentad-scale soil moisture and vapor pressure deficit during the drought, σ(VPD) is the standard deviation of vapor pressure deficit, and a smaller CSI means a stronger land-atmosphere coupling state.

Division of flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots
We optimized the method to identify flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots on the basis of previous studies 2, 5. We first defined energy-limited and water-limited regions based on the basis of the ecosystem limitation index (Figure S17a). Ecosystem limitation index was calculated by subtracting the correlation between soil moisture and evapotranspiration from the correlation between the temperature and evapotranspiration 62. An ecosystem limitation index value greater than 0 indicates a water-limited region, and an index value less than 0 indicates an energy-limited region. We then used the aridity index to divide the study regions into four large climate regions 48, including arid (aridity index < 0.2), semi-arid (0.2 ≤ aridity index < 0.5), sub-humid (0.5 ≤ aridity index < 0.65) and humid (aridity index ≥ 0.65) regions (Figure S17b). Next, we divided our study region into forest, shrub, crop and grass regions based on the vegetation type map (Figure S17c). Finally, we took the spatial intersection among the patterns of the above three global divisions into 29 regions (e.g., humid forest in energy limited region). Each region is defined by unique vegetation type, moisture and energy conditions, which means these regions exhibit different risks when facing drought stress.

We applied multivariate flash drought indicator (MFDI) to determine the flash drought hotspots 25. The MFDI can be calculated as follows:
Let X = x_ij be the matrix with n rows (representing the number of global grids) and m columns (representing flash drought ratio, counts, severity, and onset speed) and, the standardized matrix, Z = z_ij is then given as:
z_ij = 100 ± ((x_ij - M_xj) / S_xj) × 10 (3)
where Z is transformed using a common scale with mean = 100 and standardized deviation = 10, M_xj and S_xj denote the mean and the standard deviation of the jth indicator given as:
M_xj = (∑_{i=1}^n x_ij) / n (4)
S_xj = √(∑_{i=1}^n (x_ij - M_xj)^2 / n) (5)
Let cv_i be the coefficient of variation for the ith unit:
cv_i = S_zi / M_zi (6)
where M_zi = (∑_{j=1}^m z_ij) / m, S_zi = √(∑_{j=1}^m (z_ij - M_zi)^2 / m)
Then, the generalized form of MFDI is given by:
MFDI = M_zi ± S_zi * cv_i (7)
For each region, we calculated the average value of MFDI and compared it to 100. The regions with the average value of MFDI higher than 100 were defined as flash drought hotspots. Conversely, we defined as non-hotspots.

Responses of vegetation productivity to drought
We quantified the vegetation productivity responses to flash and slow droughts following a conceptual diagram (Figure S18). There are two patterns of post-drought recovery: one growing season recovery and multiple growing season recovery 48. Previous studies have shown that vegetation normally recovers within 2 years after drought disturbance 63, 64. Therefore, we discarded drought events with intervals between two droughts shorter than 2 years. We captured almost exclusively drought events where the vegetation time series showed positive anomaly before the drought’s occurrence and showed negative anomaly during the drought. We only considered the flash drought occurred during growing season and both post-drought recovery patterns of vegetation productivity. The pixel-specific growing season was determined by a pixel-specific threshold of the minimum value plus 30% of the seasonal amplitude fitting for the multiyear averaged GPP 48, 65-68. The growing season identification was further verified with SIF (Figure S19). We investigated vegetation changes within two years after drought cessation to explore the response processes of vegetation productivity to flash and slow droughts. We considered the recovery of vegetation productivity from the maximum negative anomaly point to the multi-year growing season mean state within 2 years to be the recovery process under drought effect. The resilience was quantified as the mean of vegetation anomalies after the drought effect (Y_a) minus the multi-year growing season mean (Y_m) (Equation 8) 69. A resilience value lower than 0 indicates that the effect of the drought event persists after disturbance, with lower values indicating weaker resilience.
Resilience = Y_a - Y_m (8)

Attribution analysis
We established four random forest attribution models for flash and slow droughts at flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots, respectively. In each attribution model, the importances of different factors were evaluated. We considered 15 factors in the attribution analyses, which can be grouped into 6 categories, including climate factors (spatio-temporal), CO2 fertilization effect (spatio-temporal), vegetation response features (spatio-temporal), soil property (spatial), plant trait (spatial) and stand features (spatial). All factors with temporal dimension were deseasonalized and detrended. Multiple climate factors during the drought response period (i.e., the period from the beginning of drought to the maximum vegetation negative anomaly) were considered, including the mean values of temperature, radiation, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, soil moisture and evaporation (Figure S20). Non-growing season snow anomalies could affect the spring phenology and further alter the post-drought vegetation recovery pattern across growing seasons 70. Thus, we included the non-growing season snow water equivalent. We also considered the mean values of vegetation productivity during the drought response period. Previous studies revealed that the vegetation state during the two months preceding a flash drought could compensate for the vegetation recovery process 39, 71, 72. Therefore, we also introduced the mean GPP of this period into our final random forest models. Soil property (soil cation exchange capacity), plant trait (maximum rooting depth) and stand features (canopy height and tree density) were also included in the final model. Besides, we considered the CO2 fertilization effect (β) 30, which is defined as the relative increase in vegetation productivity in response to the increase in atmospheric CO2 concentration and determined as follows:
β = ∂Productivity/∂CO2 (9)
Many studies have pointed out that the increase of CO2 can promote the plant water use efficiency 29, 73. Therefore, we included water use efficiency into the attribution analyses to assess the indirect impacts of CO2 fertilization effects on vegetation productivity resilience based on Equation 10.
WUE = Productivity / Evapotranspiration (10)
Prior to performing the final attribution models, VIF was used to test the collinearity among factors, and the factors with a larger VIF (VIF > 5) were removed to prevent the confusion effects (Figure S21a) 74.

The random forest model provides the advantages of high prediction accuracy, high robustness, accurate factor interpretation and ease of use 46. Separate random forest models were constructed to investigate the differences in the drivers underlying vegetation productivity resilience to flash and slow droughts at flash drought hotspots and non-hotspots. Here, we defined that each random forest had 300 binary trees with 5 leaves. The R2 value of the random forest attribution models were all above 0.80 (Figure S21b – e). A factor importance ranking was obtained via the permutation importance method based on Out-of-Bag data, with values normalized. The permutation feature importance method is a model inspection technique applicable for any fitted model and is especially useful for nonlinear models. The importance of permutation features is defined as the decrease in model accuracy when a single feature value is randomly perturbed. The larger the decrease after the permutation, the greater the importance of this factor 75. We selected the top ten factors as major factors for further analyses. Partial dependence plot was used to characterize the relationship between each factor and vegetation productivity resilience 76.
